title: The Milky Way’s glistening band
caption: The Milky Way over an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The glistening band of the Milky Way spans the sky over ESO's Paranal Observatory, the organisation's flagship site in the Atacama Desert. Below it, one of the Very Large Telescope's Auxiliary Telescopes still has its round dome shut, as if asleep and missing the show. Broad lanes of dark cloud cut through the band's bright core.

Those dark nebulae block the light of stars lying behind them, so those regions only seem to hold fewer stars. From the Sun's position in a spiral arm, some 25 000 light-years out from the centre, we get an excellent view of the galactic core, as Chilean astrophotographer Alexis Trigo shows here.

People long ago were unsure what this milky streak was and named it for its looks. Galileo Galilei changed that when he aimed a small telescope he had built at it and found it was made of countless stars. Today astronomers reckon it holds some 100 to 400 billion stars of every age, mass and colour.
scale: The Sun lies about 25 000 light-years from the centre of the Milky Way, according to ESO.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Alexis Trigo. The source does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the galactic core and its dark lanes may look brighter and sharper here than to someone on site.

explore: Gazing at this shining band has captivated people throughout history. Much about our home galaxy is still unknown, and ESO looks forward to whatever revolutionary findings its upcoming Extremely Large Telescope may bring.
alt: The bright band of the Milky Way crossed by dark dust lanes, above a small telescope with a closed spherical dome.
